header.html: Process Task 1 (recommend a development approach and execution strategy; determine critical information requirements) and Process Task 9 (identify and tailor needed artifacts); also "analyze and tailor communication to stakeholder needs" (People Task 4). Tailoring is the thread behind most "what should the PM do?" answers where the right choice depends on context.

toc.title: Diagnostics: Common Situations and Tailoring Suggestions (Table 3-1)
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1What Tailoring Is

Tailoring is the deliberate adaptation of the project management approach, governance and processes to align with the project's environment and objectives. It considers the development approach, processes, project life cycle, deliverables, and the approach to stakeholder and team involvement.

  • It is driven by the principles, organizational values and culture. Example: an organization with low risk appetite tends to use structured processes and oversight; one with higher risk tolerance may favor agility and decision-making autonomy.
  • Tailoring means mindfully selecting and adjusting project factors to find which elements are most useful given context, goals, operating environment, scale and complexity.
  • Projects must balance competing demands: delivering fast; minimizing cost; optimizing value; high-quality deliverables; compliance with regulations and sustainability; diverse stakeholder expectations; adapting to change.
  • Limits: organizational policy or a contract may mandate a specific approach and restrict tailoring.
Exam angle

"Tailor" is almost always better than "follow the standard process rigidly" or "drop the process." The best answer adapts within policy, justifies the change and checks that it works.

2Why Tailor?

  • There is no single approach for all projects. Structures range from extensive to minimal, rigorous to lightweight.
  • Variables: criticality, scale, duration, complexity, industry standards, organizational culture, number of stakeholders, level of organizational project management maturity. A nuclear reactor project needs far more rigor, checks and reporting than a new office building; a 10-person team needs far less coordination than a 200-person team.
  • Too few processes make management ineffective; more than required is costly and wasteful.
  • Benefits: more commitment from team members who helped tailor; stronger customer orientation (customer needs shape the approach); more efficient use of resources.

3What to Tailor

Aspect What it includes
Life cycle and development approach Choosing the life cycle and phases and the predictive, adaptive or hybrid approach. Example: a data center build with predictive construction and an adaptive approach for the computing capabilities: a hybrid at project level, though each sub-team experiences only one approach
Processes Add (unique conditions or more rigor); modify (fit needs, adjusting inputs, outputs, tools and techniques); remove (cut unnecessary cost or effort); blend (combine elements for added value); align (consistent definition and application)
Engagement People (assess skills and capabilities of leaders and team); empowerment (which responsibilities and local decisions are delegated; more supervision where capability is lower); integration (making one team from diverse contributors: contractors, channel partners, external entities, internal staff)

4The Tailoring Process (Four Steps)

4.1 Select the initial development approach

Use product knowledge, delivery cadence and awareness of options. A suitability filter is a decision-making aid (not a rigid method) that assesses culture, team dynamics and project factors to guide the choice among predictive, adaptive and hybrid, combined with other data.

4.2 Tailor for the organization

  • Teams own and improve their processes, but organizations provide methodologies and approaches as starting points for repeatable processes, consistent capability measurement and continuous improvement.
  • With process governance, align tailoring to policy; add, remove and reconfigure elements to suit the organization.
  • Consider the program and portfolio context; aligning tailoring across related projects improves consistency and efficiency.
  • A PMO often reviews and approves tailored approaches. Tailoring that affects only the project team usually needs just the project manager's approval; tailoring that affects external groups may need PMO approval. The PMO can share ideas from other projects.
  • Multi-organization projects: tailor jointly; integration planning harmonizes each organization's processes, governance and approaches.

4.3 Tailor for the project

Adjust for size, criticality and other factors by asking questions about three attributes:

Attribute Questions to ask
Product or deliverable Standards compliance (how much rigor and quality assurance?); type of product (well known like a building, or intangible like software or a drug); industry market (regulated, fast moving, slow); technology (stable or obsolescing); timeframe (weeks or years); stability of requirements; security (confidential or classified); can it be delivered incrementally and iteratively?
Project team Size (full-time and part-time); geography (remote or colocated); organizational distribution of supporting groups and stakeholders; experience (industry, organization, each other, skills, tools); access to the customer for frequent feedback; diversity of skills and perspectives
Culture Buy-in to the proposed approach; trust that the team can and will deliver; empowerment (is the team trusted to own its environment, agreements and decisions?); organizational culture (empowering vs specifying and checking; local vs external decision-making)

4.4 Implement ongoing improvement

Tailoring is not a one-time exercise. Issues with how the team works or how the product evolves signal further tailoring. Review points, phase gates and retrospectives are chances to inspect and adapt the process, development approach and delivery frequency. Keeping the team engaged in improving its process builds pride of ownership and shows trust. The way an organization tailors itself can also be tailored.

5Tailoring the Performance Domains

Each performance domain has its own tailoring considerations (listed in the topics that cover them). The principles guide behavior as practitioners tailor the domains to the project context.

Domain Where its tailoring is covered
Governance Topic 12 (governance models, approaches)
Scope Topic 15
Schedule Topic 16
Finance Topic 17
Stakeholders Topics 13 and 20 (culture, product, AI, size)
Resources Topics 19 and 25
Risk Topic 21 (size, appetite, development approach, resilience)

6Diagnostics: Common Situations and Tailoring Suggestions (Table 3-1)

Periodic reviews (retrospectives, lessons learned) show whether the current approach works. Teams without retrospectives can use issues, threats, quality metrics and stakeholder feedback.

Situation Tailoring suggestion
Deliverables are poor quality Analyze root causes and apply targeted feedback and quality assurance; focus on process improvement, not just more verification steps
Team members are unsure how to proceed Assess their specific needs and provide guidance, mentorship, training and knowledge-sharing
Team members are uncooperative and work in silos Team-building activities and individual meetings to understand the cause; strengthen bonds and coordination
Long delays waiting for approvals Streamline approvals: appoint people authorized to decide up to value thresholds
Too much work in progress and waste Value stream mapping and Kanban boards to visualize work, find issues and solutions
Stakeholders are not engaged or give negative feedback Check whether they get timely, relevant information; tailor communication methods, balancing simplicity with deeper engagement
Lack of transparency about progress Ensure the right data is collected, analyzed, shared and discussed in team and stakeholder meetings; validate agreement on the measures
Unprepared issues and risks keep surfacing Explore root causes: look for gaps in project processes or activities

7Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
What is typically tailored Level of planning detail, stage gates, control rigor, documentation, reporting Iteration length, event formats, DoD, board design, artifacts, roles Which streams use which approach, interfaces, one reporting view
Tailoring owner PM with PMO/governance within policy Team (retrospectives) within organizational boundaries PM, team leads and PMO jointly
Trigger Project size, criticality, regulation Retrospective findings, feedback, flow data Both, plus integration problems
Risk of poor tailoring Bureaucracy or insufficient control Ritual without value, or dropping needed discipline Mixed signals and duplicated effort

8Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Tailor, don't blindly apply or discard. Adapt within organizational policy; use the PMO when the change affects others; document the reasoning.
  2. Contracts and policies limit tailoring. If an approach is mandated, work within it or request an approved exception; do not unilaterally drop required steps.
  3. Fix the cause, not the symptom. Poor quality → root cause and process improvement (not just more inspection). Slow approvals → delegated authority thresholds (not pressure). Silos → team building and understanding the cause.
  4. Tailoring is continuous. Retrospectives, phase gates and lessons learned are the triggers to inspect and adapt; rigid persistence with a failing approach is wrong.
  5. Involve the team. Teams that help tailor are more committed; do not impose a process change without their input.
  6. A suitability filter supports judgment; it does not decide. Combine it with other data.
  7. Match rigor to criticality and complexity. Safety-critical or regulated work needs more control; a small low-risk team needs less.
  8. Visual flow tools for waste: value stream mapping and Kanban when work in progress and waste are the problem.
  9. Multi-organization projects need joint tailoring and integration planning.
  10. Templates and life cycles are tailored, not rewritten: the organization's master assets change only through organizational policy (Topic 01).

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1The organization mandates a stage-gate methodology, but the team on a software migration believes an iterative approach would suit the build stage. What should the project manager do?

  • ADiscuss a tailored approach with the PMO that keeps the required gates
  • BFollow the methodology in name but quietly skip the gate reviews
  • CSwitch to iterative delivery for the build stage without telling anyone
  • DRefuse to consider any change because the methodology is mandated
Show the answer

Answer: A. Tailoring happens within organizational policy and may need PMO approval when it affects groups outside the team, so the required gates stay while the iterative build is proposed. Acting silently or skipping gates breaks policy, and refusing wastes a sound idea.

S2Deliverables keep failing acceptance, and the team proposes adding two more inspection steps to its sprint workflow. What is the best response?

  • AAnalyze root causes and improve the process before adding any checks
  • BLower the acceptance criteria so that more deliverables pass
  • CIncrease the number of reviewers who sign off each deliverable
  • DAdd the two inspection steps immediately to catch defects earlier in the sprint
Show the answer

Answer: A. Table 3-1 says to analyze root causes and focus on process improvement and targeted quality assurance rather than simply adding verification steps. More inspections or reviewers treat the symptom, and lowering the criteria hides the problem.

S3On a hybrid program, approvals for small purchases take two weeks and keep delaying the iterative team. Which tailoring is most appropriate?

  • AEscalate every purchase request to the sponsor for a quick decision
  • BAppoint people authorized to approve purchases up to set value thresholds
  • CRemove the approval step completely for every purchase made on the project
  • DTell the team to start the work before the approvals arrive
Show the answer

Answer: B. Delegating approval authority by value threshold shortens delays while keeping control, as Table 3-1 suggests. Starting without approval, removing it or escalating everything either loses control or adds delay.

S4The team has many items in progress, constant rework and unclear bottlenecks. Which tailoring suggestion fits best?

  • AAdd a weekly status meeting so that progress is reviewed more often
  • BIncrease the team size so that more items can be worked in parallel
  • CExtend the schedule to give the team time to finish the open items
  • DUse value stream mapping and a Kanban board to visualize and limit work
Show the answer

Answer: D. Table 3-1 pairs too much work in progress and waste with value stream mapping and Kanban boards, which reveal where work waits and limit what is started. More meetings, people or time leave the flow problem untouched.

S5Stakeholders have stopped attending sprint reviews and now give negative feedback. Before changing the approach, what should the project manager check?

  • AWhether the schedule is on track against the release plan
  • BWhether they receive timely, relevant information in a form that suits them
  • CWhether the team needs more members so that it can prepare for the reviews properly
  • DWhether the sponsor still approves of the way reviews are run
Show the answer

Answer: B. Table 3-1 suggests assessing whether stakeholders get timely, relevant information and then tailoring the communication methods. Sponsor approval, schedule status and team size are not the likely causes of disengagement.

S6Which project factor most strongly argues for more rigorous controls and reporting?

  • AA small team of ten people who all work in the same office
  • BA familiar product whose requirements are stable and well understood
  • CA critical, regulated product with high safety consequences
  • DA short duration with a single delivery at the end of the project
Show the answer

Answer: C. Criticality, regulation and complexity drive more rigor in controls and reporting. Team size, duration and familiarity argue for lighter structures.

S7A newly formed agile team does not know how to approach unfamiliar work. What should the project manager do?

  • AReduce the scope to the parts the team already understands
  • BAssess their needs and provide guidance, mentoring and training
  • CGive them a long procedure document and let them work it out
  • DReplace the team with specialists who already know the technology
Show the answer

Answer: B. Table 3-1 suggests assessing the team's specific needs and providing guidance, mentorship, training and knowledge sharing. Handing over documents, replacing people or cutting scope does not build capability.

S8A retrospective shows that heavy documentation steps add no value on this low-risk project, but one of them is required by organizational policy. What should the project manager do?

  • ALet each team member decide individually which steps to keep
  • BRemove every documentation step, including the one the policy requires
  • CKeep every documentation step as it is because the whole process was approved earlier
  • DLighten the optional steps with team agreement and keep the required one
Show the answer

Answer: D. Tailoring works within policy and with the team's agreement: non-required steps can be lightened while the required step stays, or PMO approval is sought to adapt it. Removing everything, changing nothing or individual choice each ignores part of that.

S9Two organizations jointly deliver a system, one working in sprints and the other in phase gates, each with its own governance. What is the best way to tailor?

  • AIgnore the differences and deal with problems as they appear later
  • BLet each organization's team keep working independently with its own method
  • CTailor jointly and use integration planning to harmonize the practices
  • DUse only the larger organization's method for the entire project
Show the answer

Answer: C. Multi-organization projects need a joint approach to tailoring, with integration planning to harmonize governance and processes. Imposing one method, working separately or ignoring the gap invites misalignment.

S10Midway through the project, the team finds that its sprint cadence no longer fits stakeholder needs. What is the most appropriate action?

  • AWait until closing and record the problem as a lesson learned
  • BCancel the project and restart it with a different life cycle
  • CInspect and adapt the cadence with the team and the stakeholders
  • DKeep the cadence unchanged because it was formally approved
Show the answer

Answer: C. Tailoring is not a one-time exercise: review points and retrospectives are chances to inspect and adapt the process and the delivery frequency. Keeping an approved cadence, canceling or waiting for closing forfeits that benefit.

9.2 Recall Q&As

R1Define tailoring.

Show the answer

The deliberate adaptation of the project management approach, governance and processes to align with the project's environment and objectives.

R2What three aspects can be tailored?

Show the answer

Life cycle and development approach; processes; engagement.

R3Name the five ways to tailor a process.

Show the answer

Add, modify, remove, blend, align.

R4Name the four steps of the tailoring process.

Show the answer

Select the initial development approach; tailor for the organization; tailor for the project; implement ongoing improvement.

R5What is a suitability filter?

Show the answer

A decision-making tool, not a rigid method, that helps assess culture, team dynamics and project factors to choose among predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches.

R6Who typically approves tailoring?

Show the answer

The project manager for tailoring that affects only the team; the PMO where external groups are affected or organizational policy requires.

R7Which three attribute groups guide tailoring for a project?

Show the answer

Product or deliverable, project team, culture.

R8Why tailor?

Show the answer

Because no single approach fits all projects; it improves team commitment, customer focus and resource efficiency and avoids both too few and too many processes.

R9What does Table 3-1 suggest for long approval delays?

Show the answer

Appoint people authorized to make decisions up to certain value thresholds.

R10What triggers further tailoring during a project?

Show the answer

Issues, retrospectives, lessons learned, phase gates, quality metrics and stakeholder feedback.

R11What does Table 3-1 suggest when deliverables are of poor quality?

Show the answer

Analyze the root causes and apply targeted feedback and quality assurance; focus on process improvement, not just more verification steps.

R12What does Table 3-1 suggest for too much work in progress and waste?

Show the answer

Use value stream mapping and Kanban boards to visualize the work, find the issues and identify solutions.

R13What does tailoring the engagement cover?

Show the answer

People (assess the skills and capabilities of leaders and team), empowerment (which responsibilities and local decisions are delegated) and integration (making one team from diverse contributors).

R14What limits tailoring?

Show the answer

Organizational policy or a contract may mandate an approach; templates and life cycles are tailored for the project, while the organization's master versions change only through organizational policy.

10Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Tailoring Deliberate adaptation of approach, governance and processes to environment and objectives
What Life cycle and approach · processes · engagement
Process tailoring Add · modify · remove · blend · align
Engagement tailoring People · empowerment · integration
Four steps Select approach → organization → project → ongoing improvement
Suitability filter Decision aid (culture, team dynamics, project factors)
Approvals PM for team-internal; PMO if external groups are affected; policy and contracts can restrict
Project attributes Product/deliverable · team · culture
Poor quality Root cause + process improvement
Approval delays Delegated authority by value threshold
Too much WIP/waste Value stream mapping + Kanban
Stakeholders disengaged Check information relevance; tailor communication
Ongoing Retrospectives, gates, lessons learned → inspect and adapt
First-action pattern Understand context, adapt within policy with the team, check it works, keep adjusting
